cards.q: What do you use Zotero (or similar) for in research work?
cards.a: Reference management: store sources, organise a literature survey, and generate citations/reference lists (APA7 / course requirements).

figure.caption: Zotero stores sources and builds citations
figure.shows: Reference managers keep PDFs/metadata and generate APA reference lists.

cards.q: Name three sensible steps in a literature search (as the course trains).
cards.a: 1) Clarify topic/question and search terms. 2) Search relevant databases and sort/categorise hits. 3) Critically assess sources and build a taxonomy/spreadsheet for the essay.

figure.caption: Literature search is a clear process
figure.shows: Question -> search -> assess -> write and cite.

cards.q: What is IMRaD, and when is it used?
cards.a: Introduction-Methods-Results-and-Discussion: common structure in empirical research articles. The ACIT4100 essay is not a typical IMRaD literature review-it should understand and communicate research in a classic/narrative style.

cards.q: What distinguishes a claim from evidence in academic text / Toulmin?
cards.a: A claim is what you assert; evidence/data supports the claim. The Toulmin model (used in the course's rhetoric/ethics assessment) separates claim, data/grounds, warrant, and more.

cards.q: Why is peer review important?
cards.a: Quality control before publication: other researchers assess method, argumentation and contribution-a central part of the publication tradition you should describe in the essay.

figure.caption: Peer review checks quality before publication

cards.q: What characterises a good research question for this course?
cards.a: Scoped, relevant to ACIT/your specialisation, researchable via literature (not anthropological fieldwork), and suited to make methods, ethics and the research field visible-not just a 'technology product'.

figure.caption: A clear research question keeps the essay focused
figure.shows: One evaluable question beats a vague theme dump.

cards.q: When must you cite in academic text?
cards.a: When you use others' ideas, data, wording or unique content-including when paraphrasing. Missing citation = plagiarism of ideas/words. The course requires an APA7-based standard.

cards.q: What is the 2026 essay focus shift in ACIT4100?
cards.a: Away from mainly describing a technology, toward understanding and communicating research: methods, history/tradition, notable researchers/venues, regulation/ethics, industry/society relations-summarise and synthesise others' work, not invent new empirical findings.

figure.caption: Essay = communicate research clearly
figure.shows: Focus the question, use quality sources, synthesise and cite.

cards.q: Which writing styles must the ACIT4100 essay mainly use?
cards.a: Classic style (Steven Pinker, covered in the course) and/or narrative style (short-story techniques). Hybrids (classic with narrative 'cut-scenes') are allowed. Style cannot compensate for thin research content.

cards.q: How does ACIT4100's referencing standard differ from plain APA7 for scientific papers?
cards.a: Based on APA7 but stricter for scientific papers: include page number and paragraph number. Books/websites follow conventional APA7. See Kildekompasset APA 7th.

cards.q: Which assessment categories are weighted most heavily (***) in the essay rubric?
cards.a: Literature survey (***) and Research methods (***). Rhetoric and Flow/structure are **; Ethics **; Visual presentation and Language/other are *.

cards.q: What literature volume is discussed in assessment / failure criteria?
cards.a: Rubric: ~10 research articles is low, ~20 is high (how they are used matters more). Failure risk if fewer than 10 research papers. The course plan notes a mandatory spreadsheet survey (threshold can differ by document year-follow current Canvas/2026 requirements).

cards.q: What AI declaration is required, and what happens if it is missing?
cards.a: At the end of the essay (after the reference list): list tool(s) and activities, OR state that no AI was used. Not in the word count. Using AI is not mandatory for a good grade. Missing the Declaration of AI use means fail, whether or not AI was used. OsloMet: https://student.oslomet.no/en/veiledning-kunstig-intelligens-studentoppgaver

figure.caption: Declare tools or non-use
figure.shows: After references; not in word count.

cards.q: When is using AI treated as cheating in the ACIT4100 essay?
cards.a: Using AI to literally write parts of the essay is cheating. The exam requires you to write the essay; generated text is not writing and tries to circumvent the exam.

cards.q: Give four examples of AI use that count as cheating for the essay.
cards.a: 1) AI writes the essay/parts from your ideas. 2) AI fixes up your draft. 3) AI generates an essay from your material. 4) AI restyles your paragraph into essay style. All leave text that was not really written by you.

figure.caption: AI must not write your essay text

cards.q: Why does AI-generated essay text often get weak grades, beyond integrity?
cards.a: LLM text often reads bland, polished and business-like - little personality - and says little despite fancy language. It also short-circuits learning to understand and communicate research, which you develop by writing yourself.

cards.q: Which AI uses does ACIT4100 endorse for the essay process?
cards.a: Summarise/explain research articles; group articles into categories; have AI summarise YOUR draft/outline so you check coverage against your ideas; discuss topic/structure; help find material / common knowledge; teach grammar/writing from YOUR paragraph so YOU improve. Mentoring support - not masking your writing.

figure.caption: AI as mentor, not ghostwriter
figure.shows: Support learning; do not write for you.

cards.q: Is Grammarly (or similar spell/style checkers) cheating in ACIT4100?
cards.a: Not cheating if they only work on text you write yourself. Not endorsed either: they often make wording overly advanced/academic. Rare synonyms do not improve the text.

cards.q: Name major plagiarism forms from the Avoiding Plagiarism reading.
cards.a: Verbatim (word-for-word / mosaic); plagiarism of ideas (paraphrase without credit); self-plagiarism/duplicate publication; loose paraphrasing that keeps another's logic; failing to cite non-scholarly sources that contributed unique information.

cards.q: What are the two mandatory goal-posts before the essay exam (from saved course pages)?
cards.a: 1) Assignment 1 - Literature taxonomy spreadsheet (scientific papers threshold for approval). 2) Assignment 2 - Presentation recording (5-10 minutes on the essay topic). Exact due dates: verify current Canvas (year labels may lag).

cards.q: Give examples of weekly themes from the saved ACIT4100 syllabus.
cards.a: Rhetoric & persuasive arguments; searching/sorting literature; philosophy of science; research methods; using AI for research; classic style; narrative templates; public speaking; role of the expert; plagiarism; Q&A.

figure.alt: Weekly themes feeding the research funnel
figure.caption: Syllabus topic examples

cards.q: What should the ethics discussion in the essay cover (assessment criteria)?
cards.a: Identify ethical issues (professional ethics, research ethics, societal impact); present different viewpoints; de-construct arguments. The course plan also requires ethical challenges of research and societal uses.

cards.q: List key reasons an essay may fail (from assessment information).
cards.a: Missing AI-use declaration (fail); insufficient research literature (minimum 10 considered); cannot follow evaluation criteria; insufficient research focus; not technology-related; no standard referencing; too much rewrite of sources ('not your own text'). Common word-count/cheating rules still apply; list not complete.

figure.alt: Integrity failures that can fail the essay
figure.caption: Declaration and plagiarism risks

cards.q: What is the ACIT4100 essay word count (current Canvas)?
cards.a: Individual essay 5500-6500 words (A-F). Not group work. Old intro video may still say ~12000 words - that is outdated. Confirm on current Canvas / OsloMet course page for your year.

cards.q: Which three content blocks must the ACIT4100 essay include (course plan)?
cards.a: 1) Literature survey. 2) Discussion of methods used in the reviewed material. 3) Ethical challenges (research ethics and societal uses).

cards.q: What literature spreadsheet threshold should you follow for Mandatory 1?
cards.a: Current Canvas: taxonomy spreadsheet with 10+ scientific papers. Older saved course plans mentioned at least 7 - always follow the threshold published on current Canvas.

cards.q: What is the video goal-post before the essay exam?
cards.a: A 5-10 minute recording/presentation on the essay topic (mandatory work requirement).

cards.q: Are you expected to produce new empirical findings in the ACIT4100 essay?
cards.a: No. Summarize, synthesize and communicate what others have published; you are not trained as anthropologists inventing new fieldwork models.

cards.q: For scientific papers in ACIT4100 APA7-based referencing, what extra detail is required?
cards.a: Include page number and paragraph number (stricter than plain APA7). Books and websites follow conventional APA7. See Kildekompasset APA 7th.

figure.alt: APA citation with page and paragraph
figure.caption: Stricter for papers

cards.q: Name the main Toulmin parts used in the course's rhetoric/ethics work.
cards.a: Claim (assertion), data/grounds (evidence), and warrant (why the evidence supports the claim); further parts may include backing, qualifier, and rebuttal.

cards.q: Does paraphrasing remove the need to cite?
cards.a: No. Using another's ideas or unique content in your own words still requires citation; otherwise it is idea plagiarism.

cards.q: What authorship convention is named in the ACIT4100 learning outcomes?
cards.a: The Vancouver convention on authorship (who qualifies as an author) - part of research integrity and publishing tradition.

cards.q: What method families should you be able to discuss when reviewing papers?
cards.a: Qualitative and quantitative research methods (and how papers in your field typically design experiments/labs or studies) - identify methods used in the literature you survey.

cards.q: Give examples of philosophy-of-science themes listed for ACIT4100.
cards.a: Falsificationism/paradigms and traditions within philosophy of science (explicit or implicit in a research field) - connect them to how your field publishes and argues.

figure.alt: Philosophy of science in the funnel
figure.caption: Paradigms and falsification

cards.q: List example perspectives the 2026 essay requirements suggest for describing a research field.
cards.a: Methods/methodologies; lab/experimental designs; philosophy-of-science tradition; publication venues; history of the field; codes of conduct/regulation; industry/society relations; ethical effects.

cards.q: Where does the course point you for APA 7th details?
cards.a: Kildekompasset APA 7th (Norwegian and English): https://www.kildekompasset.no/en/referencing-styles/apa-7th/

cards.q: What is 'classic style' in this course (Pinker / Sense of Style)?
cards.a: Clear, reader-oriented prose as described by Steven Pinker (The Sense of Style) and covered in class - suitable for popular-science / expert communication. May be hybridised with narrative cut-scenes. Pinker's book is on the optional source list (not pensum), but classic style itself is course-relevant for the essay.

cards.q: What is the current ACIT4100 course name, and what outdated title may still appear in old video?
cards.a: Current: Understanding and Communicating Research. Old intro video may still say Research methods & Ethics - treat that title as outdated; trust Canvas.

cards.q: Who teaches ACIT4100 now (current Canvas)?
cards.a: Kyrre Begnum and Sylvia Lysgård. Older materials naming Pedro / Kristine are outdated.

cards.q: How does the flipped classroom work in ACIT4100?
cards.a: Study the digital material BEFORE class. Class time is for activities and assisted individual work (not a first-time lecture of the week's content).

cards.q: Is attendance mandatory, and what classroom rules apply?
cards.a: Attendance is NOT obligatory - you do not need to notify staff if absent. Sessions are built for active participation / group work. If you come, arrive on time; breaks and meals are outside the classroom.

cards.q: How far ahead do teachers publish weekly digital material?
cards.a: At least one week ahead, so you can prepare before class.

cards.q: Is the ACIT4100 exam group work, and what length should you ignore from old video?
cards.a: No - it is an individual essay (5500-6500 words on current Canvas). Old video length ~12000 words is outdated. Not a group exam.

cards.q: Is the ACIT4100 essay a typical literature review?
cards.a: No. It is not a typical literature review - write to the published assessment criteria (methods, ethics, communicating research, etc.), not a generic review template.

cards.q: What is Assignment 1 (official Grades name), and when is it roughly due?
cards.a: Assignment 1 - Literature taxonomy spreadsheet (10+ scientific papers threshold). Due around 26 September as listed on Canvas (Canvas/Grades may show 2025 / year quirks - always verify the year for your course run).

cards.q: What is Assignment 2 (official Grades name), and when is it roughly due?
cards.a: Assignment 2 - Presentation recording (5-10 minute video on the essay topic). Due around 31 October (confirm exact date/time and year on Canvas).

cards.q: When is the essay exam roughly due?
cards.a: Around 5 December at noon on Canvas for the current run - always verify the exact deadline and year on Canvas / OsloMet (do not treat a pasted year as absolute truth).

cards.q: How should you plan time for the ACIT4100 essay?
cards.a: Writing takes weekly time across the semester - do not leave the full essay for the final weeks after the mandatory goal-posts.

cards.q: What English level is expected in the essay?
cards.a: Plain, grammatically correct English is enough. Advanced / fancy language is not an advantage in assessment.

cards.q: Where do you find formal exam details (word count, form, year)?
cards.a: OsloMet course information page for ACIT4100 - select the correct academic year. Cross-check Canvas for work requirements and deadlines.

cards.q: If old intro video conflicts with Canvas (name, teachers, word count), what do you trust?
cards.a: Trust current Canvas and the OsloMet course page for your year. Intro video can lag (old course title, old staff, old ~12000-word length).

cards.q: What is class time mainly for in ACIT4100?
cards.a: Active participation and group work: activities plus assisted individual work on your essay/literature process - after you have already done the digital prep.

cards.q: What may you choose as the ACIT4100 essay topic (Essay requirements 2026)?
cards.a: A field of research of your own choosing within the scope of the ACIT program. Focus on the research itself (understanding and communicating research), not mainly a technology with research around it.

figure.alt: Choose a research field within ACIT
figure.caption: Own research field within ACIT
figure.shows: Topic = research field, not a product pitch.

cards.q: Should you judge the quality of research findings like a domain expert?
cards.a: No. Search, summarize, synthesize and communicate what others have published. You may discuss how you interpret findings, but you are not expected to judge their quality as an expert. You are not trained anthropologists uncovering new knowledge.

figure.alt: Synthesize do not judge as expert
figure.caption: Report and interpret, do not referee
figure.shows: Communicate published knowledge; do not act as expert referee.

cards.q: Who decides which essay perspectives are more mandatory than others?
cards.a: The assessment criteria document: clear expectations prescribe some areas as more mandatory. You choose the mix of perspectives, but you must check that document and cover the prescribed priorities.

figure.caption: Check the criteria document
figure.shows: Mix is yours; mandatory weight comes from the rubric.

cards.q: Do weekly course materials alone cover the essay perspectives?
cards.a: No. Weekly content gets you started on most topics, but you still need substantial own effort, including skill training in reading scientific works. Class also includes writing exercises.

figure.caption: Course starts; you deepen
figure.shows: Prep + own reading + in-class writing drills.

cards.q: Can excellent style compensate for thin research content in the essay?
cards.a: No. Style is only a wrapper around information that must be communicated. Best grades go to essays that are rich in content and well executed in classic and/or narrative style.

figure.caption: Content first, style wraps it
figure.shows: Rich research content + well executed style.

cards.q: Is ACIT4100 hybrid (online + campus in parallel)?
cards.a: No. The course is not hybrid - expect on-campus sessions for participation/group work (plus the flipped digital prep before class).

cards.q: Are ACIT4100 class sessions recorded?
cards.a: No. Classes are not recorded so students can speak more comfortably and so learning from participation stays in the room.

cards.q: How do you access research articles for ACIT4100 (library FAQ)?
cards.a: Search Oria via the OsloMet library (https://www.oslomet.no/en/ul) - log in; use VPN or the OsloMet network when needed. Google Scholar often works too.

cards.q: Where do you hand in the ACIT4100 exam?
cards.a: Inspera via Studentweb - see https://student.oslomet.no/hjemmeeksamen for home-exam / Inspera access guidance.

cards.q: Where do you find your candidate number before the exam deadline?
cards.a: In Studentweb - look up your candidate number there before the hand-in deadline.

cards.q: What should you know about course video captions and browsers (Canvas FAQ)?
cards.a: Closed captions (CC) are English-only (speech recognition). Supported browsers: Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari. Allow pop-ups so video tools work.

cards.q: What happens if you fail the ACIT4100 essay exam?
cards.a: A continuation exam (konte) is available. It counts as a new exam attempt. Reasons for failing are listed in the assessment information document.

cards.q: If you failed ACIT4100, can you keep working on the same essay for the continuation exam?
cards.a: Yes. Failed students may continue working on the same essay they submitted. How much rework is needed varies.

cards.q: If you passed ACIT4100 but want a better grade next year, can you improve the same essay?
cards.a: No. You must submit a new essay. Unlike failed students on konte, you cannot improve the same base text.

cards.q: How long do previously approved mandatory assignments stay valid when retaking ACIT4100?
cards.a: Only for the past two years. If older, you must redo them.

cards.q: Why is sharing your ACIT4100 essay with other students a breach?
cards.a: The essay is an individual exam. Sharing it with others breaks exam rules. Official OsloMet cheating info: https://student.oslomet.no/en/cheating

cards.q: Is plagiarism from sources allowed if you do not share your essay with classmates?
cards.a: No. Plagiarism from sources is also forbidden - do not present others' text or ideas as your own without proper citation.

cards.q: How does OsloMet check electronic essay submissions for cheating?
cards.a: Submissions are checked against the internet and other exams (including previous years and courses). The system can detect synonym swaps and systematic rewriting.

cards.q: What is the process if cheating is suspected at OsloMet?
cards.a: A report is made; the student is notified and invited to a meeting; the case goes to a central committee; then a judgment is issued.

cards.q: What penalties can follow an OsloMet cheating judgment?
cards.a: Acquittal; annulled grade (must retake the course); or annulled grade plus expulsion from all Norwegian higher education for up to 1 year. In ACIT4100, experience is that cheaters often get the strongest penalty.

cards.q: How do ACIT4100 teachers help with writing about others' research?
cards.a: They help you write ABOUT others' work - not write what those authors write. You must produce your own wording and understanding.

cards.q: What caution does the essay assessment information give about using the star list?
cards.a: Do not try to calculate your grade from the list (you lack other essays). Do not reverse-engineer category weights with example essays - the list is revised yearly. Stars are coarse relative importance only. Rubrics may feel unclear early; meaning grows during the course. List = what they look for, not how to execute well.

figure.caption: Stars guide; do not reverse-engineer grades
figure.shows: Relative weight only; list evolves yearly.

cards.q: What do the stars (*, **, ***) mean in the ACIT4100 essay rubric?
cards.a: Coarse relative importance when grading: *** weighs more than **, which weighs more than *. Not a full hidden points formula. Categories: Literature survey *** and Research methods ***; Flow/structure **, Rhetoric **, Ethics **; Visual presentation * and Language/other *.

cards.q: How many sensors read each ACIT4100 essay, and what may compensate?
cards.a: Two sensors read each essay. Strong performance in one category may sometimes compensate for weaknesses elsewhere - but structured criteria still aim for transparency.

cards.q: What does Flow / structure (**) look for in the essay?
cards.a: Easy to follow with guiding text: paragraphs stick to one topic/point; introduction communicates the focus; segues (transitions) between sections; coherent overall structure.

figure.caption: Topic paragraphs, intro focus, segues
figure.shows: Guide the reader; keep a coherent path.

cards.q: What does Rhetoric (**) look for in the essay?
cards.a: Rhetorical and dramatic devices plus appropriate style: capture attention in the introduction; rhetorical devices; dramatic devices for interest/engagement; use rhetoric terminology and the Toulmin model (e.g. how others frame an issue, or in ethics); written in classic style.

figure.caption: Attention, devices, Toulmin, classic style
figure.shows: Rhetoric ** includes classic style and Toulmin.

cards.q: Beyond paper count, what does Literature survey (***) reward?
cards.a: How papers are used matters more than raw count (~10 low, ~20 high). Aggregate and categorize articles; use categorization to highlight aspects/observations; add non-scientific material (media, podcasts, dictionaries) for context; present literature in a storyline order.

figure.caption: Categorize, contextualize, storyline
figure.shows: Use > count; build a narrative path through sources.

cards.q: What does Research methods (***) require in the essay?
cards.a: Identify key research methods/approaches in your literature; describe them; discuss some (background, paradigm, strengths and weaknesses); give examples of how papers in your survey used the method.

cards.q: What does Visual presentation (*) require?
cards.a: Images/diagrams share a consistent visual format, including titles and captions. Visuals complement written text - they must not replace it. Do not drop diagrams without advising the reader how to understand them.

figure.caption: Consistent captions; complement text
figure.shows: Same format; guide the reader; do not replace prose.

cards.q: What does Language / other (*) cover, and which reference styles are mentioned?
cards.a: General English proficiency, plus proper quotes and referencing. The language bullet says must follow IEEE or APA. Primary course standard for ACIT4100 is still APA7-based and stricter for scientific papers (page + paragraph). Books/websites: conventional APA7. See Kildekompasset.

figure.caption: English + quotes/refs; APA7-stricter primary
figure.shows: Language * mentions IEEE or APA; course primary = APA7-stricter for papers.

cards.q: Do books and websites need page and paragraph numbers under the ACIT4100 referencing standard?
cards.a: No. The stricter page + paragraph rule applies to scientific papers. Books and websites follow conventional APA7.

cards.q: Which signs may lead to reporting the essay for cheating (assessment information)?
cards.a: List not complete. Signs of circumventing collect-organize-structure-write with own skills: text-generation engines; masking others text as your own; using text/images/content without reference; using paper lists from other literature reviews instead of your own searches. Ask staff if unsure.

figure.caption: Own search, own writing, proper credit
figure.shows: Generators, masking, no refs, borrowed paper lists.

cards.q: What is "not your own text" as a fail reason (distinct from plagiarism)?
cards.a: Too much of the essay is merely a rewrite of other sources. May not be plagiarism in mild cases, but sensors cannot find enough of you composing with your own writing skills - so the essay can fail on that basis.

figure.caption: Rewrite-heavy text can fail
figure.shows: Compose; do not only rephrase sources.

cards.q: What literature minimum can lead to considering a fail?
cards.a: Fewer than 10 research papers: sensors will consider failing. Rubric also treats ~10 as low and ~20 as high, but how papers are used matters more than count alone.

cards.q: Name research-focus and topic fails from the assessment information.
cards.a: Consider fail if: cannot evaluate against the criteria list; insufficient research focus; not related to technology; no standard reference format. Also fail if missing AI declaration or under 10 research papers (see other cards).

figure.caption: Research + technology + evaluable criteria
figure.shows: Stay on research/technology and meet the rubric.

cards.q: What does a literature "storyline" mean in the survey criterion?
cards.a: The order in which you present literature should show a deliberate narrative path - not a random dump of papers. Storyline supports coherence with Flow/structure.

figure.caption: Ordered path through the literature
figure.shows: Sequence = argument, not a pile of cites.

cards.q: May you use non-scientific sources in the literature survey criterion?
cards.a: Yes - to substantiate, complement, or give useful context to the research literature (e.g. media articles, podcasts, dictionaries). They support, not replace, research articles.

cards.q: What is the primary referencing standard for ACIT4100 essays?
cards.a: APA7-based, mandatory for every essay regardless of writing style. Stricter for scientific papers (page number AND paragraph number). Books/websites: conventional APA7. Language rubric mentions IEEE or APA for quotes/refs, but the course primary standard is this APA7-stricter rule. Details: Kildekompasset APA 7th.

figure.caption: APA7-based + page and paragraph for papers
figure.shows: Primary course standard; IEEE/APA note is secondary in Language *.

cards.q: Why do teachers share the star criteria instead of only example essays?
cards.a: They grade something slightly different from a normal literature survey. Example texts can help but also confuse when topics/styles differ. The star categories help you self-evaluate against what sensors look for.

cards.q: Is the Canvas "List of source material" mandatory pensum for ACIT4100?
cards.a: No. The course has no single textbook. The listed books/talks are NOT part of the curriculum; they are optional deeper material ordered by topic (Writing, Philosophy of science, Political philosophy, Rhetoric, Technology and Society), not by importance.

figure.caption: Source list = fordypning, not pensum
figure.shows: No single textbook; dive deeper only if useful.

cards.q: What is Freytag's Pyramid useful for in ACIT4100 essay styles?
cards.a: A classic narrative arc (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, denouement/resolution). Useful if you write in narrative / short-story style or use narrative cut-scenes inside classic prose. Listed under Writing on the optional source list - craft tool, not a book to memorise as pensum.

figure.caption: Freytag-style story shape
figure.shows: Shape tension for narrative essay sections.

cards.q: How do narrative templates relate to the ACIT4100 essay (vs memorising every Writing source)?
cards.a: Syllabus week on narrative templates supports short-story techniques and hybrids with classic style. Optional Writing sources (e.g. Olson on narrative, Freytag's Pyramid) can deepen craft; you do not need to memorise the full source list as if it were pensum.

cards.q: For scientific papers in ACIT4100, which locators must citations include?
cards.a: Both a page number and a paragraph number (or a line range when that fits better). The Overleaf example shows how to attach these locators in LaTeX citations.

figure.alt: Citation with page and paragraph locators
figure.caption: Page + paragraph (or lines) for papers
figure.shows: Course rule: scientific papers need precise locators, not only author-year.

cards.q: Which packages does the ACIT4100 Overleaf APA example emphasise, and how is biblatex set up?
cards.a: csquotes and biblatex. Configure biblatex with style=apa and backend=biber (plus sorting options as in the example). Document style and spacing can change; those packages are the important part.

cards.q: In the Overleaf example, when do you use parencite versus textcite (with optional locators)?
cards.a: parencite = parenthetical citation. textcite = narrative citation (author names in the sentence). Both can take a locator such as [\pno~17, para.~3] before the bib key.

cards.q: Is hansen2024 in the Overleaf referencing example a real paper for your essay?
cards.a: No. It is an illustrative bib entry (fake DOI) only to demonstrate page/paragraph locators - not a source you should treat as real research.

cards.q: Where is the compiled APA_example.pdf for the Overleaf referencing demo?
cards.a: On the ACIT4100 Canvas page Referencing example for OverLeaf / LaTeX (download APA_example.pdf there). The page also shows the LaTeX/bib setup.

cards.q: Why must you pass the Mandatory information quiz in ACIT4100?
cards.a: It must be passed to open the rest of the course in Canvas. (Course information quiz is separate; both appear under Grades.)

cards.q: What is the official Canvas/Grades name of Assignment 1 in ACIT4100?
cards.a: Assignment 1 - Literature taxonomy spreadsheet. Due around 26 September noon on Canvas (dates may still show year 2025 - verify the year for your run).

cards.q: What is the official Canvas/Grades name of Assignment 2 in ACIT4100?
cards.a: Assignment 2 - Presentation recording. Due around 31 October noon on Canvas (dates may still show year 2025 - verify the year for your run).

cards.q: What is psychological acceptability in Saltzer and Schroeder (1975)?
cards.a: Protection mechanisms must be easy enough that people will actually use them - security that humans reject in practice fails. A founding usable-security idea before the field had a name.

cards.q: What did Zurko and Simon (1996) name?
cards.a: User-centered security - connecting Saltzer-style human factors to a research program inside security, not only HCI.

cards.q: What is the main claim of Adams and Sasse (1999) "Users are not the enemy"?
cards.a: Blaming users as the weakest link ignores design and organisational causes shown in interviews - poor usability and policy drive many breaches, not an "enemy within".

cards.q: Why is "Why Johnny can't encrypt" (Whitten and Tygar, 1999) canonical?
cards.a: Usability evaluation of PGP 5.0: unusable crypto is insecure crypto. Introduces cognitive walkthrough-style evaluation for security tools.

cards.q: What is Zurko's (2005) "grand challenge" for usable security?
cards.a: Usable security as a cross-disciplinary scientific challenge - not password tips but evidence, venues, and methods - ahead of SOUPS institutionalising the field.

cards.q: What is SOUPS in usable security history?
cards.a: Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security - first held 2005 (Cranor general chair), growing from CHI/WUPSS workshops into a refereed venue for the field.

cards.q: Name principles from Krol et al. (2016) for robust security user studies.
cards.a: Include realistic primary tasks and risk, avoid priming, and design experiments so findings reflect real behaviour - five principles summarised for LASER; field standard for empirical usable security.

cards.q: What must a usable-security essay be about (Karina Spine A / course rules)?
cards.a: The research field itself (canon, venues, methods, ethics) - not phishing training as main topic, not SOC job tips, not new empirical mini-master or IMRaD lab report.

cards.q: ACIT4100 exam essay word count?

cards.q: Course information quiz (ACIT4100): which teaching model is named?

cards.q: Course information quiz (ACIT4100): mandatory work and exam format?

cards.q: Mandatory information quiz (ACIT4100): which AI use is cheating?
cards.a: Using AI to write or rewrite parts of your essay. Explaining a paper with AI, Grammarly grammar checks, or discussing your topic with a classmate are not listed as cheating in that question.

cards.q: Mandatory information quiz (ACIT4100): which AI tools are allowed?
cards.a: Tools that help you understand material and improve your own writing (not tools whose main job is to create fluent English for you, and not a blanket ban on all generative AI).

cards.q: Mandatory information quiz (ACIT4100): where must AI use be declared in the essay?
cards.a: In a declaration of use after the references section.

cards.q: Mandatory information quiz (ACIT4100): how does flipped classroom work here?
cards.a: You study the material before class and work on exercises during class time.

cards.q: Mandatory information quiz (ACIT4100): why two mandatory assignments before the essay?
cards.a: They act as goalposts so you stay on track toward the essay (not graded components replacing the exam).

cards.q: Mandatory information quiz (ACIT4100): which writing style is encouraged for the essay?
cards.a: Classic style (as described by Steven Pinker) - not legal/bureaucratic tone or narrative short-story style.

cards.q: How is the Toulmin model split in ACIT4100 Canvas videos?
cards.a: Five parts: (1) why debates matter, (2) the model, (3) arguing affirmative, (4) arguing negative, (5) debates as decision-making. Each has a self-test quiz.

cards.q: What does flipped classroom mean in ACIT4100 Canvas?
cards.a: The lecture is the homework. Class time is joint and individual work with the teacher. Get through digital material before the week. Teachers publish at least one week ahead.

cards.q: Name ACIT4100 in-class principles from the flipped-classroom page.
cards.a: Professional inclusive focus; breaks and meals outside the room; attendance not mandatory but arrive on time if you come; students prep digital material; staff publish a week early.

cards.q: What eight craft points did the ACIT4100 first lecture list under Text is good?
cards.a: Curiosity, metaphor, humour, foreshadowing, visualization, tell a story, conclusion, give the reader a break. Craft only: they do not replace sources or a research claim.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what three signs mark a good argument?
cards.a: Persuasive (effective in getting support for a claim). Uses deliberative rhetoric (focus on the future and what to do next, not judicial or epideictic). Relevant (relates to the question that is debated).

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what is deliberative rhetoric in a good argument?
cards.a: Focusing on the future and what to do next. A good argument uses this, not judicial or epideictic rhetoric.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: who developed the Toulmin model, and what was it based on?
cards.a: Stephen Toulmin, an English philosopher interested in what makes everyday arguments successful. The model was based on reviewing court cases. It is now widely used to construct and de-construct arguments (debate, research, essays, dinner tables, cocktail parties).

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what is the prime function of the Toulmin model?
cards.a: Not to describe the order of the argument, but that the right components are in place to make it persuasive.

figure.caption: Right components, not a fixed order
figure.shows: The model checks that the pieces that make an argument persuasive are present.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2 smoking example (Kyrre Begnum): what are the claim and the grounds?
cards.a: Claim: You should stop smoking. Grounds: Smoking leads to severe health risk for yourself. Smoking can affect the people around you.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2 smoking example: what are the explicit and implicit warrants?
cards.a: Explicit: You cannot disregard the advice of the medical community. Implicit: You should take health advice from your friends seriously.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2 smoking example: what backing, qualifier and rebuttal appear on the diagram?
cards.a: Backing: We know what happens to people who ignore unanimous advice from doctors. Qualifier: At least try to reduce it as much as possible and set a goal to stop before a date. Rebuttal: I know it is difficult, but there are other products that can help you control the nicotine addiction.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what is a claim in the Toulmin model?
cards.a: What you want your audience to accept: opinion, action, vote, support and so on. It can be for or against a proposal.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: when might you not see a claim even if the rest of the Toulmin model is there?
cards.a: Especially in scientific and technical presentations: the claim can be missing from view even though the other parts are present.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what can grounds be, and what should they do?
cards.a: Evidence, data, statistics, anecdotes. They should present the reasoning behind the claim. They may also contain evidence of expertise or authority.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: why are grounds the backbone of the argument, and why might they still fail?
cards.a: Grounds will most likely be the backbone of the argument, but they may affect people differently based on factors like their own emotional investment.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what provides the core of your grounds in research?
cards.a: The results and their analysis.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what is a warrant, in simple terms?
cards.a: Why you should listen to me. The warrant can itself be a longer argument. Warrants can be data and evidence, or values.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what is fascinating about the warrant?
cards.a: It helps put the argument in a context. It can help explain why the same claim and grounds work differently in different settings.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what changes when the smoking example is aimed at a spouse instead of a colleague?
cards.a: The implicit warrant changes with the audience. Colleague: you should take health advice from your friends seriously. Spouse: you should respect the concerns and advice from those who love you. Claim, grounds, explicit medical warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal stay the same idea.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: why use a qualifier instead of an unqualified claim?
cards.a: An unqualified claim would have to be defended for all extreme cases.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: how can qualifiers adjust the guarantee of success?
cards.a: With wording such as most likely, greatest chance, or 90% of ...

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: how can qualifiers insure against insufficient grounds?
cards.a: With wording such as considering all other options, after careful deliberation, or given what we know right now.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what does actual listening mean for debaters?
cards.a: They spend their time keeping track of the debate, instead of thinking about what they want to say next.

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: how can the Toulmin model help you listen?
cards.a: As a structure by which to categorize what you hear (and do not hear).

cards.q: Week 2 Part 2: what is flow in debate, and how are flows made?
cards.a: A technique that lets you quickly note what is being said in a system that makes line-by-line refutation possible. Flows are created with symbols that signify meta-information of the arguments.
